common_name: Meteor Shower Verbena (Compact Non-Seeding Tall Verbena)

planting.note: Set out container-grown transplants after all danger of frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; this vegetatively propagated selection sets very little seed compared with the open-pollinated species, so it stays where it is planted instead of colonizing nearby beds.

directions: Meteor Shower grows into a denser, more rounded bush than the tall, airy, often floppy species or the groundcover-like 'Lollipop', building a self-supporting mound roughly two feet tall and under a foot wide that rarely needs staking. Clusters of small violet-lilac flowers top wiry stems continuously from early summer to frost, drawing steady traffic from butterflies and hummingbirds throughout the display. Because this selection produces very little viable seed, it avoids the aggressive self-sowing that limits some gardeners' enthusiasm for the wild species while keeping the same drought and heat tolerance once established. Grow in full sun to very light shade in average, evenly moist, well-drained soil for the fullest bloom.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, keeping the mix evenly moist under strong light since germination is naturally slow and uneven; transplant into lean, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed.

directions: Vanity is a seed-raised breeding advance rather than a vegetatively propagated patented selection like 'Lollipop' or 'Little One', yet it still trims the wild species down to a tidy, well-branched two-to-two-and-a-half-foot mound instead of a tall, lanky stand. Wiry, angular stems carry dense clusters of vivid violet-purple flowers from summer well into fall, and the compact scale suits both mixed borders and patio containers. Its performance in North American and European seed trials earned it both an All-America Selections award and a Fleuroselect Gold Medal, a distinction from most other verbena in this dataset. Once established it tolerates hot, dry spells with ease and remains a strong draw for butterflies and hummingbirds all season.

common_name: Angelface Steel Blue Angelonia (Silvery Lavender-Blue Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts after the last frost in full sun and well-drained soil; Steel Blue runs taller than most other Angelface colors, so give it room at the back of a bed or the center of a large container.

directions: Angelface Steel Blue carries pale, silvery lavender-blue flowers on extra-large spikes, a softer and cooler tone than either the deep purple-and-white bicolor of Angelface Wedgwood Blue or a true saturated blue, and it noticeably outgrows most series-mates, often reaching two and a half feet. The semi-upright, well-branched habit and faint grape-soda fragrance are shared with other Angelface selections, and spent flowers drop cleanly without deadheading. It shrugs off the heat, humidity, and drought that stress cool-season spike flowers like true snapdragons, blooming from late spring through the first hard frost. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching and feed on a regular schedule to sustain the long bloom run.

common_name: Angelface Blue Angelonia (True Blue Early-Flowering Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts after the last frost in full sun and well-drained soil; Angelface Blue begins flowering roughly one to two weeks earlier than most other colors in the series, so buds often appear while nearby Angelface selections are still filling out.

directions: Angelface Blue delivers a clear, saturated true blue on its large snapdragon-like spikes, a more vivid and warmer-toned blue than the pale, silvery cast of Angelface Steel Blue already covered here. Growth is a dense, well-branched mound typical of the series, and this particular color is noted for reaching bloom noticeably ahead of its series-mates in spring. It shares the Angelface line's outstanding heat and humidity tolerance and self-cleans without deadheading, holding color and form through the peak of a Gulf South summer. Pinch once while young to build a fuller frame, and expect steady, uninterrupted bloom from that early spring flush through the first fall frost.

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Serena Blue is a true-blue color option within the same compact, seed-grown Serena breeding line as Serena Purple already cataloged here.

directions: Serena Blue fills the cool end of the seed-grown Serena color range with clear blue-violet spikes, giving growers a distinct color choice alongside the deep purple of Serena Purple within the same compact, uniform, early-flowering breeding line. The narrow, glossy foliage carries a faint grape-like scent when brushed, and the well-branched, tidy habit needs no pinching to fill out a pack or bed. Like other Serena colors it thrives rather than merely survives through the hottest, most humid stretch of a Gulf South summer, blooming continuously from planting to frost without deadheading. Water when the top inch of soil dries and expect reliable, low-maintenance performance all season.

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Serena White has shown notably better resistance to phytophthora root and crown rot than many other seed-grown angelonia colors, an advantage in beds that drain slowly after summer downpours.

directions: Serena White produces clean white spikes on the same compact, well-branched frame as Serena Purple and Serena Blue, rounding out the seed-grown Serena line with a bright, neutral color that pairs easily with almost any companion planting. Beyond its color, this selection stands out within the series for holding up better against phytophthora crown and root rot, a real advantage during wet, humid Gulf South summers when soggy soil can quickly take down less resistant angelonia. It blooms continuously from planting through frost without deadheading, tolerating the punishing heat and humidity that stall true snapdragons. Give it full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil, and expect vigorous, disease-free performance through the entire warm season.

common_name: Serenita Sky Blue Angelonia (White-Throated Sky Blue Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 8-9 plant March-May. Serenita is bred for a naturally compact, well-branched habit that fills a pot or bed without pinching.

directions: Serenita Sky Blue carries clear sky-blue flowers set off by a contrasting white throat, giving each small snapdragon-like bloom more visual depth than the solid-colored Serenita Pink already in this dataset. The PanAmerican Seed introduction keeps the Serenita line's naturally compact, tidy, self-branching habit, so plants fill out a pack or border position without pinching. It is self-cleaning and blooms continuously from late spring through frost, thriving in the heat and humidity that cause true snapdragons to decline. Grow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and expect strong drought tolerance once the plants are established.
